1.pericope_label: The congregation weeps, wishes itself dead, and moves to elect a captain back to Egypt

schools.summary: Gill limits the first outcry to the princes and elders standing by when the report came in, though he expects word to spread and raise a general clamour; on the proposed election he notes that they already had captains over the tribes and wanted one commander over all, and that Nehemiah speaks as though the appointment were actually made, their will being taken for the deed. Calvin sees how easily a few incentives raise sedition in a multitude, which left to itself is like a sea open to every tempest. He grants a pretext — ten chosen men dissuading and only two advising — but will not excuse the credulity, since it grew out of incredulity: if the standing of ten men weighed so much, how much more the word of God, who had promised that land four centuries before. He argues the wish to have died against the old interpreter, who took the optative particle for a negative and made them say their death in the wilderness would be bitterer than in Egypt, whereas their complaint is of the death they expect ahead. On the charge itself he is harshest of all: they accuse God of deception and cruelty, as if he were betraying them to the Canaanites, and of weakness besides, repaying his kindnesses by calling him their betrayer.

Henry lays the mischief at the door of the ten, supposing the twelve had talked the matter over before reporting and that Caleb and Joshua did their utmost to bring the rest round — had the others but let Caleb speak for them all, nothing would have come of it; instead the ten seem to have designed the mutiny deliberately, against Moses and Aaron, though they could propose no gain unless they hoped to command the retreat. The wish to have died he treats as causeless discontent: never had months been spent so pleasantly as those since Egypt, loaded with honours and favours, yet they would rather have perished with the firstborn or with those lately struck down for lusting, choosing to die criminals under God's justice than live conquerors in his favour. It is unbridled passion, he says, that makes men prodigal of the one thing nature holds dearest; they wish to die for fear of dying, without the sense of the lepers who reasoned that if their enemies killed them they should but die. He notes also that some render the words as a present wish.

Clarke draws a character of the people: with scarcely any firmness of mind and almost no religion they bore no reverse and were forever at their wit's end, headstrong and pusillanimous by turns — and because they were such, the power and wisdom of God stand out the more in their story. The proposal to choose a captain he calls a formal renunciation of Moses and flat rebellion, and marvels that men whose lives had been embittered by Egyptian rigour should be eager to return, past evils weighing less than present ones far smaller. Wesley adds the grim sequel to their wish, that they had it before long and did die in that wilderness; observes that from the instruments they rise higher and strike at God, the author of the journey, which shows how fast sin grows unresisted; and presses the folly of the plan — who would cover them with a cloud, feed them with manna, bring them over the sea, or answer for their welcome among the Egyptians they had ruined?

Ellicott marks the revolt as now open against Jehovah himself, to whom they impute the exodus by way of reproach; he would render the question as a present one, wherefore doth the Lord bring us into this land, and identifies the danger they feared as the sword of the Amorite and the Anakim rather than famine. Keil calls it a murmuring that grows into open revolt.

5.pericope_label: Moses and Aaron fall on their faces, Caleb and Joshua plead, and the congregation calls for stones

schools.summary: Gill offers three readings of the prostration — shame at so shocking a proposal, an appeal to the people to lay the thought aside, or a supplication that God would convince them of their folly. Calvin doubts whether they humbled themselves before the people or fell in prayer, and prefers the second, as a rebuke of their stupidity by turning to God: in such obduracy nothing was left but to call on him, yet openly, since a retired place would have served had prayer alone been the point. The rending of garments he explains as an eastern usage, solemn in extreme grief or in abhorrence of a crime, which hypocrites afterwards imitated to feign sorrow or deceive the simple, though here it was genuine; and he observes that Joshua's courage is now named where before only Caleb was praised. On the plea he fastens on the conditional particle: some take it as causal, that because God loves us he will bring us in, which he rejects as foreign to the sense — the doubt is put in not to weaken hope but to bring them to repent, and the words only rebel not show that nothing shuts up God's way but their own refusal to obey. He is unsurprised at the stoning, since men who have censured God will rage against his servants, reproof of iniquity ending at last in fury; and notes that God does not argue or threaten but displays his power, rescuing them as from wild beasts. Gill holds with Ellicott that the congregation ordered to stone them must mean the princes and chief men, there being otherwise nobody to address the order to.

Henry takes the prostration as all three of Gill's readings at once, and adds a practical reason: the noise was such that they could not be heard, and calling for silence would have made the crowd louder, so they gained a hearing by falling down in sight of the assembly — praying God to still the noise of that sea, showing the trouble of their own spirits as men astonished to see a people fling away their mercies. The rending of garments he refers to the spies' share in the commission, which made the tumult theirs, their colleagues having raised the storm. On the plea he admires the reasoning: they commend the land as very, very good, so the word runs, giving no ground to despise so pleasant a place — men convinced of the gains of religion would not stick at its services. He makes light of the walled cities: though the Canaanites are fortified they are naked, that common providence which guards the rights of nations having abandoned them, and no people can be safe when they have provoked God to leave them, while Israel, though in tents, is fortified, the Lord being there and his name a strong tower.

Wesley reads the prostration as the refuge Moses always took in such straits, done before all the assembly that the sight might awaken them, and refers the rent garments to grief at the blasphemy and sedition and the judgment they foresaw. The figure of eating them as bread he turns practically — we shall destroy them as easily as we eat bread — and warns that nothing can ruin sinners but their own rebellion, since if God leaves them it is because they drive him away. Clarke notes with Ellicott that the defence departed is literally a shadow, a figure of force in hot countries where shelter from the sun is worth much, and adds that Arabs and Persians use the same word; from the rescue he draws the moral that a man is immortal till his work is done.

Ellicott gives the same literal sense of the departed shadow, and holds that the iniquity of the Canaanites is now full and themselves ripe for destruction. He agrees with Gill that the congregation bidden to stone them must be the princes and chief men, adds that Moses had feared the same violence before, and places the appearing of the glory in the court rather than the tent, since the people could not otherwise have seen it.

11.pericope_label: How long will this people provoke me: the threat of pestilence and the prayer that turns it

schools.summary: Calvin fixes on the obstinacy, that they had rejected God with atrocious insults in the face of the clearest proofs of his power. He is unsure of the verb, doubting the rendering provoke and thinking Jerome nearer with how long will they detract me, but rests on the plain drift, which the next clause confirms: God complains of being disparaged, since they will not weigh the miracles that testified his power and kindness, refusing credit to a heap of signs that ought to have broken their stubbornness; and the words how long, he adds, measure both the length of the crime and the patience of God. On whether the threat was absolute he meets the difficulty head on: it may offend that God should pronounce the people cast off when their pardon was already decreed, but he is not speaking of his secret counsel, only of what they deserved and of the vengeance hanging over them, his design being never to keep Moses from praying but to prove the fervour of his zeal. Yet he will not let the comfort run far, adding that though God is placable by nature, the hope of pardon is justly cut off from men so obdurate that neither his hand nor his word makes any impression. Gill observes that the pestilence did fall, but on the spies who brought the evil report, and holds that as to the body of the people the words are partly a proposal to draw Moses out, partly a threatening to bring the nation to a sense of its sin.

Henry reads the summons as a vindication: while the people were busy disgracing Moses, God called him to the tabernacle and put public honour on him as the man of his counsel. He gives the verb its range — they provoke, or reject, reproach and despise, because they will not believe — and makes unbelief the bitter root, distrust of God's power being itself a great provocation and lying at the bottom of many others; heaven keeps account of how long men hold out, and the longer they hold the greater the offence. He finds two aggravations, that they were a peculiar and professing people, the nearer to God in name the more provoking their sins, and that they had seen every sign shown among them. The sentence he states without softening: what remains but to make a full end, smite them with pestilence, blot out name and race — they wished to die, and they may die; and if it is asked what becomes of the covenant with Abraham, the answer stands in the same breath, that it will be kept in the family of Moses. This he takes for a trial, whether Moses still preferred Israel's interest to the advancement of his own house; and it appears he was of the same public spirit and could not bear to raise his name upon the ruin of theirs. The sin had made a fatal breach in their defence, through which destruction would have entered had Moses not stepped in — here a type of Christ, who prayed for his persecutors — and since the pardon of a national sin consists in turning away the national punishment, that is what the one word Pardon is earnest for.
Wesley calls the threat not a determination but a commination, of the same kind as the sentence on Nineveh, with a condition implied — unless there be speedy repentance or powerful intercession.
Ellicott notes that the same promise of a greater nation was made at the rebellion at Sinai, and that Moses interceded then in the same way.

13.pericope_label: Then the Egyptians shall hear it: the appeal to the name, and the plea for great power

schools.summary: Gill notes that the plea begins abruptly, Moses being greatly disturbed by the threatening; on the petition for great power he offers two senses, either that the power shown in the exodus and the wilderness might appear greater still in bringing them into the promised land, or else that there might be a great display of pardoning grace — for as God's power appears in his forbearance towards the wicked, much more in forgiving them, there being more virtue in grace to pardon than in sin to damn; and he takes the longsuffering of the recited titles as reaching all men and especially God's own. Calvin has Moses stand in the breach of the wall, as the psalm says, resting his whole request on one thing, that God's holy name would become the sport of the wicked if the nation perished: Egypt will hear, since it is notorious that this people was rescued from them by his might; the report will pass to the Canaanites, who already know him for their protector; and if they perish now, every nation that has heard his fame will conclude that his power broke down in mid course, unable to finish what it began. From this he draws a caution, that the tie serves us only if we plead it sincerely, since many boldly urge God's name on their own behalf who care nothing for it, and the more signal his past power the more insolent the blasphemy if it seems to fail. He looks past the phrase about great power to its source, that Moses draws his confidence from the vision in which God had declared his own nature, and makes it a general rule that nothing in prayer is more effectual than to set God's word before him and build the request on his promises, as though he had dictated what we should ask. On the closing petition he is full: Moses sets before himself the greatness of God's mercy and then the past proofs that he is inclined to forgive, for though iniquities heaped on iniquities might justly frighten us, the abundance of grace should swallow up all dread of wrath; and because a bare acknowledgment of that goodness is often not enough, he adds the stay of experience — pardon, as thou hast so often pardoned already — which Calvin makes the most effective importunity of all.

Clarke thinks the passage needs no explanation, and calls the arguments pointed, cogent and respectful, showing a heart full of humanity and the deepest concern for the divine glory. Wesley allows only one sense for the petition for great power, the words that follow restraining it: pardon is the single instance described in the divine titles, asked by Moses, and granted in the answer — nor is it strange that pardon should be called an act of power, being an act of omnipotent goodness. He also raises a difficulty of his own, why Moses should quote the clause about visiting iniquity on the children, which looks like an argument for destroying rather than sparing; one answer is that he would not sever what God had joined, but the truer answer, he thinks, is that the words should be rendered otherwise — that in destroying he will not utterly destroy, though he visit the iniquity of the fathers on the children.

20.pericope_label: I have pardoned according to thy word: the oath, the glory, and the ten temptings

schools.summary: Gill takes the plain sense with Clarke and Wesley, that the nation was not utterly cut off, and reports the Jerusalem Targum's reading that the Word of the Lord remitted and forgave, which he refers to Christ, since none but God can forgive sin; he notes too that God swears by his own life, having no greater. Calvin asks how God can spare men whom he determined to punish to the utmost and did shut out of their inheritance, and answers that the pardon was granted not to the individuals but to their race and name, rejecting as unnatural the opinion that the men themselves were released from eternal death because God was satisfied with a temporal penalty: Moses was heard so far and no further, that Abraham's seed should not perish and the covenant not fail. On the glory filling the earth he notes that some render the clause in the past tense, of a glory already displayed in many miracles, which chimes with the next words about men who have seen that glory, but prefers the future, God calling to witness the glory he is about to assert — Moses having feared that the nation's ruin would become a reproach, and God now swearing to vindicate his name so that the guilty shall not go unpunished. Of the ten temptings he will have no counting: the number is not fixed, and God means only that they provoked him without measure or end. He also defines the offence, that to tempt God is to subject his power to the narrow rule of our senses and prescribe how he shall act to suit our desires, the root being a refusal to listen to his voice, since nothing but obedience restrains our insolence.

Henry makes the answer a testimony to prayer: God had designed a pardon, but Moses is to have the praise of obtaining it, a whole nation rescued by one man's importunity — Pardon, says Moses; I have pardoned, says God. In the glory filling the earth he hears an answer to the very thing Moses had pleaded for, that all the world shall see how God hates sin even in his own people and how gracious he is, as when our Saviour prayed, Father glorify thy name, and was answered that it had been glorified and should be again; those who sincerely seek God's glory may be sure of what they seek. The ten temptings he counts, reckoning this exactly the tenth occasion on which the congregation had provoked God — the Red Sea, Marah, the wilderness of Sin, Rephidim, the calf, Taberah and Kibroth-hattaavah — and remarks that heaven keeps a tally.

Clarke and Wesley agree with Gill on the plain sense of the pardon, that the nation was not utterly cut off. Clarke narrows the glory filling the earth to the land: all this land, that is Canaan, fulfilled to the letter only when the preaching of Christ and his apostles was heard through all the cities of Judea, the globe not seeming to be meant wherever the expression occurs. Wesley narrows it differently, to the report of God's righteous acts in punishing this people.

Ellicott balances both sides of the pardon: justice required the transgressors to be overtaken, yet the prayer was heard and the people not exterminated. He reports a reckoning of the ten temptings like Henry's, made up by adding two transgressions over the manna to the eight recorded murmurings, but thinks it likelier that ten stands, as elsewhere, for a full measure; and he identifies who fell under the sentence — those numbered in the first census, Joshua and Caleb and all under twenty excepted, and any others belonging to Levi, neither numbered then nor represented among the spies. Keil explains Caleb's exemption: another spirit was in him, not the unbelieving yet proud temper of the mass but obedience and trust, so that he fulfilled to walk behind Jehovah with unwavering fidelity, and for that the land he had walked over was promised to him and his seed.

22.pericope_label: Turn you into the wilderness: Caleb's portion, the ambush in the valley, and the sentence on the numbered

schools.summary: Gill offers two guesses why Caleb alone is named — that Joshua had no children, so nothing could be said of his seed possessing the land, or that as commander he needed no separate mention. On the Amalekites he takes it that their settled home was the mountain and they had come down to sit in the valley in wait, and finds goodness in the warning of a people who had provoked him. He reports the rabbinic reading that the evil congregation means the ten spies, whence ten make a congregation, and that the murmuring is causative, but judges the whole people meant. Calvin grants that Joshua shared the grace but holds Caleb specially distinguished, as the man who lifted the banner first and encouraged his colleague; and though he allows that the word for another spirit is sometimes used of a mere disposition, he has no doubt divine inspiration is meant, praising a man who not only exhorted others but went forward undeterred while the world was convulsed about him. On the parenthesis he canvasses three constructions and prefers a fourth, that the words are a reproach: Israel had come to the border of the inhabited land, where the enemy might have been routed, and God now turns them out of ground they had reached. The repetition of the sentence to Aaron as well as Moses he marks as no new matter but a driving home, hears the opening as an angry interrogation and what follows as bitter irony — nothing was further from their wish than to wander in the desert, yet God will gratify them in a sense they never meant — takes the lifting of the hand for a form of swearing, as though God were called from heaven to witness and judge, and finds the sharpest reproof in this, that their self-will should annul, so far as they were concerned, a promise he had ratified by oath. Yet he notes the mercy folded into the threat, that the children they had lamented over as a prey are the very ones to be given the land.

Wesley reckons Joshua not among the people at all, an attendant on Moses and no more to be counted with them than Moses and Aaron; and on the other spirit he makes it another temper, faithful and courageous, moved not by the cowardice ruling his brethren but by the Spirit of God. Clarke will not have it a natural boldness but the influence of heaven lifting Caleb above earthly fears, and renders the next phrase literally, that he filled up after God.

Ellicott sets out the difficulty of the parenthesis: the words may join to what precedes, so that Caleb's seed should possess the land those nations occupy, but he objects to that and to taking the clause as plain geography, which suits the hill better. Since the verb often means a temporary sojourn, as of Joshua's ambuscade, he would render it that they are abiding in the valley — lying in ambush, which is Ibn Ezra's reading and gives the command its force: do not walk into the snare, but turn away. He notes with Keil that the sentence in the later verse has no verb, and would supply pardon or forgive from the earlier prayer. Keil reads the parenthesis instead as a plain reason for the order, identifies the valley with the broad Wady Murreh running into the Negeb, where the Amalekites were nomads while the Canaanites held the hills, takes Canaanite as the general name for the Amorites, calls the verbless sentence an aposiopesis and supplies the same words as Ellicott; and he sets out the terms of the sentence — every man numbered from twenty upward should fall there, Caleb and Joshua excepted, while the little ones would be brought in to know the land their fathers despised.

33.pericope_label: Forty years for forty days: the wandering, the breach of promise, and the death of the ten

schools.summary: Gill renders the word for wandering as feed, as shepherds who never rest but move on for fresh pasture, and holds with Ellicott and Wesley that the forty years run from the exodus and not from the spies' return, a year and a half having already passed. Calvin makes the shepherd a figure for a sojourner with no settled residence, quoting Hezekiah's complaint that his lodging is departed like a shepherd's tent, and explains the whoredoms metaphorically: God having espoused this people, by rejecting his worship they broke the vow like gadding harlots. He faces what the sentence does to the innocent — God visits the fathers' sins on the children and yet chastises nobody undeservedly, since the sons who bore another's fault were not themselves guiltless — and finds mercy even in the delay, God waiting till the children had the strength of manhood. On the disputed clause he finds the versions various, some making it, ye shall know whether I am false, and takes it for an ironical concession by which God reproves a pride whose aim had been to charge him with falsehood. He will not allow that the death of the ten is recorded out of order by anticipation: Moses has finished the general sentence and now sets down the spies' particular punishment, so that God begins with them and their unnatural death becomes a presage to the rest. He presses two words — the plague, implying they did not die in the course of nature, and before the Lord, which means more than in his presence, God executing judgment as though he had ascended the tribunal.

Henry places the death of the ten before the sentence was published and draws two lessons from it. God marked his displeasure against men who both sinned and made Israel sin: they had slandered the land of promise, and those greatly provoke him who misrepresent religion, painting his service as mean or unprofitable; and as ring-leaders they might expect a particular mark of wrath. The survival of the other two he thinks the most striking part — all twelve probably stood together, and when ten fell dead of an infectious distemper the two among them were untouched, which confirmed their testimony and confounded the men who had talked of stoning them.

Clarke sets the two forties together, the spies searching forty days and the people wandering forty years, and would have them make a captain and go back to Egypt if they can, God having hedged them so that they could neither return nor advance. The clause about knowing God's breach of promise he calls most harsh, and reports that learned men would render it my vengeance, with the Septuagint and Vulgate behind them — the sense being that God, having promised on condition of obedience, was no longer held by a covenant they had broken. Wesley keeps the covenant language but turns it back on the people: as they first broke the compact by breaking its terms, God makes it void on his side by withholding what was promised, so that the charge of breach of promise they had brought against him is seen to lie at their own door; and he reads the whoredoms as the punishment of that apostasy from a Lord who was their husband.

Ellicott would render the word for wandering as that they shall be shepherds, and confirms the reckoning of the forty years from the later numbering, after Aaron's death. On the disputed clause he looks to the word itself, which occurs elsewhere only in Job, though the cognate verb is common in this book for refusing or disallowing, and settles on rejection or alienation. Keil renders it God's turning away, and sees in the sudden death of the ten a practical proof of the threat, a stroke from before Jehovah falling visibly on the men who raised the revolt while their two colleagues were left alive.

39.pericope_label: The people mourn, presume, and are discomfited unto Hormah

schools.summary: Calvin allows it a just cause for weeping to hear that a longsuffering they had wantonly abused would hereafter be inexorable, but sets it down as the sorrow of the world that worketh death, where the wicked weep and yet never cease to murmur, gnawing the bit with more obstinacy and rushing like untamable beasts into blind despair; no tears could redeem a temporal punishment, the one remedy being to submit and calmly undergo it, whereas they struggle proudly to shake it off and under a pretence of submission prepare to advance, wanting their confession accepted as satisfaction. In the reply of Moses he hears a rejection of feigned penitence, the sinner trying every shift rather than submit; and to the objection that the people had no other remedy he answers that banishment from Canaan was no disinheritance from the hope of eternal life, and that by this misdirected activity they doubled the evil. He denies that they meant to array themselves against God, holding rather that they hoped to appease him by offering their lives up, the zeal of the wicked being fervent when it ought to be still and dead when he commands; their senselessness appears in leaving the ark and Moses behind and running forward like doomed men. Gill has them up early, in as great a haste to possess Canaan as they had lately been to return to Egypt, names the order they broke — to turn back toward the Red sea — cites the Targum that the ark, the tabernacle and the cloud of glory did not move, and reports the Vulgate rendering that being darkened they went up, referred by some to understandings given over to blindness and by others to a march before daylight, with an old exposition making them go obscurely because they went without leave. On the name he follows Jarchi, that Hormah is called from this slaughter, or from the later destruction of the Canaanites and so given by anticipation, or from both; the Targum makes it no name but a word, even unto destruction.

Henry takes the sudden eagerness as duty mistimed turned into sin, and wishes men were as earnest for heaven while the day of grace lasts as they will be after it; they had distrusted God's strength and now presume upon their own without it.

Wesley grants the grief but says it came too late, there being now no place for repentance, and adds that such mourning there is in hell, though the tears will not quench the flames; on the last verse he says only that the Canaanites here are strictly the Amorites, and that the place was so called afterwards from this slaughter. Clarke marks the contradiction: lately they thought that with Omnipotence on their side the land could not be conquered, and now imagine that without God they can drive out its inhabitants — fallen nature runs to extremes, by turns presumptuous and desperate.

Ellicott finds from what follows that the sorrow was for the punishment the sin entailed, not godly sorrow for the sin; renders the phrase as towards the top of the mountain, takes the route for the one the spies had used, and observes that the closing verses imply they never reached the summit. He adds that Moses already had the word of the earlier verse and knew the visible token would not go, puzzles with Gill over the enemy's position — whether they had left the valley, posted a party to hold the pass, or are different portions of the same nations — thinks the enemy met them before ever they gained the summit, and points to the article, the Hormah, the place of the ban, judging a common name likelier to mark three different places than one to be meant proleptically.
